analysis.one_liner: Blocks big local phone companies from merging unless the Justice Department and FCC find it would help competition.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate hearing or vote; it died in the Judiciary Committee at the end of the 105th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the largest local phone companies — those serving more than 5% of U.S. telephone lines — from merging with or taking control of each other unless the Attorney General found the merger would promote competition and the FCC found the companies had fully opened their networks to rivals as required by the 1996 telecom law. It gave federal courts power to block deals that failed those tests and required the Justice Department to report to Congress on each approved merger's competitive effects.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of local and long-distance phone service, and the smaller competing phone companies that were trying to enter local markets after the 1996 Telecommunications Act. The bill aimed to keep a handful of regional phone giants from buying each other up and re-creating local monopolies, and to make sure big companies had actually opened their networks to competitors before being allowed to merge.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Phone customers and smaller competing carriers

how_it_helps.text: It would bar any local phone company serving more than 5% of U.S. access lines from merging with or acquiring another such company unless the Attorney General found the deal would promote competition for telephone exchange and access services [S2][S3].

It would require the FCC to find that each merging company had fully implemented its 1996 telecom-law duties to interconnect with and open its network to competitors — covering at least half of its access lines in each state, at least half of which must be residential lines — before the deal could go forward [S2][S3].

It would give U.S. district courts jurisdiction to block prohibited mergers and authorize the Attorney General to sue for injunctive relief when a deal fails the competition or network-opening conditions [S2][S3].

It would require simultaneous applications to both the Justice Department and the FCC, a deadline for decisions, and a Justice Department report to the Judiciary Committees analyzing each approved merger's effect on competition [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The large regional telephone companies (and their affiliates) that wanted to consolidate, which would face a new legal bar to mergers among the biggest players and a higher showing — an affirmative pro-competition finding plus proof of full network opening — before any deal could close. Their shareholders bore the cost of foregone merger premiums and of litigation if deals were challenged.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large regional phone companies and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The bill targeted only one narrow slice of the telecom market — mergers among the very largest local phone companies — leaving out cable companies, long-distance carriers, wireless providers, and smaller local carriers, so consolidation could simply shift to unregulated combinations [S2][S3].

The compliance test was bureaucratic: a merger could still be approved if the Attorney General made a favorable finding and the FCC certified network opening on at least half the lines in each state, so half-interconnected companies could clear the bar [S3].

Some would argue the FCC and antitrust agencies already had authority under the Communications Act and Clayton Act to review these mergers, and adding a mandatory prohibition-with-exceptions structure could slow deals or duplicate existing review rather than improve outcomes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real and timely problem: the late-1990s wave of consolidation among the regional Bell companies threatened to re-concentrate local phone markets just after the 1996 law promised competition. Its safeguards were targeted and retained existing antitrust and FCC authority [S3]. The main weaknesses are its narrow scope — covering only the largest local carriers and letting mergers proceed if FCC network-opening duties were met on the covered lines — and the possibility that consolidation would simply move into combinations the bill does not reach. On balance it would likely have modestly helped consumers and competing carriers at a real cost to the biggest incumbent companies.

outcome.mechanism: A senator introduced it, the Senate sent it to the Judiciary Committee, and it later went to that committee's antitrust subcommittee, but it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Leahy introduced the bill on June 23, 1998; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
On October 13, 1998, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust and Business [S5].
It had no cosponsors [S4], and the bill's final action in the record is the subcommittee referral; it died in committee when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large regional telephone companies benefited: without the new merger barrier, they remained free to pursue consolidation under existing, more discretionary antitrust and FCC review, and no court could automatically block deals among them.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy (D-VT)
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont (bill sponsor, Judiciary Committee member)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; the bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee, on which he serves

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no organized opposition [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would bar mergers among companies serving more than 5% of U.S. access lines and condition any deal on an affirmative Justice Department competition finding plus FCC certification of full network opening — a hard constraint on a consolidation strategy. Consumers would gain if it prevented re-concentration of local phone markets; the companies would lose deal options and merger premiums.

industries.industry: Competitive local exchange carriers and other telecom entrants
industries.note: As potential merger targets excluded from the bill's ban, they kept their independence, and any large-carrier merger would require proof the big companies had opened their networks to interconnection under sections 251-252 of the Communications Act — the access entrants depend on. Their interest runs with consumers' interest in local competition.
